request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the pediatric emergency with confusion and disorientation. She was diagnosed with bacterial meningitis based on clinical examination and CSF analysis and was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin. A CT scan was performed, and pneumocephalus was observed in the right frontal region. The patient was treated for signs of chronic sinusitis and pansinusitis. She showed initial symptomatic improvements to antibiotics but suffered a deterioration of her GCS to 7/15, with a high-grade fever.

Subdural empyema was diagnosed through a repeat CT scan, requiring immediate neurosurgical intervention. The surgical drainage was performed, and on the second day, the patient's GCS improved to 15/15, and her fever had subsided. The patient was discharged with a prescription for oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient received intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin to treat bacterial meningitis. Subdural empyema was treated through immediate neurosurgical intervention, which involved surgical drainage. The patient was prescribed oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants upon discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen at two-week and four-week follow-ups and experienced significant improvements in symptoms.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode involves bacterial meningitis, then subdural empyema as a complication, with sinusitis as the likely source. The principal diagnosis is the condition established after study to be chiefly responsible for the admission. The surgical drainage was for the subdural empyema, which was the main focus of treatment, and it is intracranial abscess/empyema from sinusitis.

In ICD-10, intracranial abscess is G06.0 (intracranial abscess and granuloma), which includes subdural empyema. G06 is coded as a "G" category, and a note says to use an additional code (B95-B98) to identify the infectious agent. Meningitis is G00 (bacterial meningitis, not elsewhere classified). When both meningitis and abscess are present, the combination is coded to G06.0 as intracranial abscess with meningitis.

The sinusitis is the likely underlying source, but intracranial abscess is the main condition treated, and the sinus condition was chronic and managed with discharge medications only. The subdural empyema was the reason for the surgery and the most resource-intensive condition. Therefore G06 is the best choice.

CODE: G06
